utterance: Hi Daniel, I'm Dr. —, thanks for coming in. I understand you've hurt your lower back lifting over the weekend and you're keen on an MRI. Before we talk about any scan, can you tell me what happened and how you've been since?
reply: I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden on Saturday and felt a twinge, then woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed, so it has been three days now. It is low down on the left side of my back and sometimes goes into my left buttock, and it is worse when I bend or get out of a chair, though it feels a bit better lying still with a heat pack and gets worse by the evening. I have worked from home the last two days, mostly lying on the couch with my laptop, and I can walk around slowly.

utterance: Good news first, Daniel: the examination shows nothing worrying. Your nerves, leg strength, reflexes, sensation, and bladder and bowel control are all completely normal, and you have no fever or tenderness over the spine itself. What you have is a muscle and ligament strain in your lower back (what we call simple or mechanical low back pain), which is the commonest cause and usually settles over a few weeks.
reply: If it is just a strain, why do I still feel like I can barely move after three days? Surely an MRI would tell us exactly what is wrong so we can be sure it is safe.

utterance:
That's a very reasonable question, and I understand why you'd want the certainty of a scan. But I'm going to explain why an MRI isn't the right test right now.

The reason you can barely move is that the muscles around your lower back have gone into spasm to protect the injured area — it's painful but it's not dangerous. Three days in is often when it's at its worst.

An MRI is extremely detailed, but for uncomplicated back pain it's actually unhelpful and can sometimes do more harm. In people your age without any nerve or "red flag" symptoms, MRI very often shows "wear and tear" changes like bulging discs that are completely normal and nothing to do with your pain. Those incidental findings can lead to worry, or even to unnecessary procedures. The best evidence-based guidelines advise that a scan is not needed in the first six weeks when there are no alarm symptoms — and you have none.

So I'm confident an MRI is not needed today. If the pain doesn't improve, or if any new symptoms appear, then I would absolutely arrange further imaging. Let's instead focus on what will actually get you better.
reply: If you are really confident I do not need a scan, I suppose I can hold off for now, but I really just want to know what I should be doing to get over this quickly.

utterance:
The main message is: keep moving. Bed rest longer than a day or two actually slows recovery, so try to stay as active as you can within your comfort. Gentle walking is great, and go back to normal activities and work as soon as you feel able — avoiding heavy lifting for now. Movement, even if slightly sore, won't cause damage.

For the pain, I'll give you some medication. Regular anti-inflammatory and simple paracetamol together works well. I'll also talk through heat or ice, which you're already using.

It's also worth being realistic: most people with this type of back pain are much better within two to four weeks, though a bit of discomfort can linger — that's normal and not a sign something is wrong.
reply: I can try to take those medications, though I really hope I start improving soon because being stuck like this is incredibly frustrating.

awards.label: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times daily with food, short course
Paracetamol as the analgesic

utterance:
I've prescribed two things for you to take together, and they're safe to combine:

- Ibuprofen 400 mg, three times a day, with food (to protect your stomach).
- Paracetamol 1 g (two 500 mg tablets), up to four times a day.

Take the ibuprofen with food, and stop it if you get any stomach pain, heartburn, or notice dark/bloody stools. Don't take more than the advised amount of paracetamol. Take both only as needed for the next five days or so, then use them only on bad days after that.

Keep using the heat pack, and gentle walking is your best medicine — little and often. Try to return to work and normal activities as you can. Avoid heavy lifting, twisting, and prolonged lying down.
reply: Thank you, I will take the ibuprofen with food and keep using the heat pack while trying to go for some gentle walks.

utterance:
One more important part — here's when to come back or seek urgent care, because these would be new signs that need checking:

- Numbness around your bottom or inner thighs, or new difficulty controlling your bladder or bowels.
- New weakness, numbness, or spreading pain down one or both legs.
- Fever, chills, or feeling generally unwell.
- Pain that keeps getting worse despite treatment, or any unexplained weight loss.

I'd also like you to book a review with me in about two weeks if it hasn't clearly improved, and we can reassess then — and at that point, if things aren't settling, we can talk again about whether any imaging is warranted. But right now I'm confident that's not needed.

Does all of that sound reasonable to you?
reply: That sounds reasonable, but honestly, I have been reading about slipped discs and people needing surgery, and I figured I would need an MRI to see what is going on, especially since the pain is about a seven when I move or roll over, though maybe a three if I keep still.

awards.label: What he is worried the pain might be
What he expects from the visit

utterance:
I hear that worry — a lot of people have it, and reading online only makes it bigger. Let me reassure you on the "slipped disc" point specifically.

Even if there were some disc change inside (which we'd expect to see in many people your age with no symptoms at all), the key fact is that the overwhelming majority of disc problems — even actual nerve irritation — settle completely with exactly the conservative treatment I've described, without any surgery. Surgery is only ever considered for a small minority, and only when there are clear nerve signs like leg weakness, severe leg pain, or loss of bladder control. You have none of those: your leg strength, reflexes, and sensation are all perfectly normal, which is a very strong sign you do not have anything that needs a scan or an operation.

The important thing is that an MRI today would not change how I treat you — and the treatment would be the same either way. That's another reason we hold off. If, on review, you developed any nerve symptoms, then imaging and a specialist opinion would come into play.

Your pain score of 7/10 on movement is consistent with a nasty muscle spasm, and it will ease as the spasm settles over the next days to weeks.
reply: That makes sense, and I appreciate you explaining it so clearly. I will fill those prescriptions, use the heat pack, and try to keep moving.
